title: Homework 1 — The Analysis of Analysis
instructions: Untimed practice. Answer each question in a few complete sentences, in your own words.

problems.prompt: A student says in seminar: "The sentence 'nothing is a square circle' must be talking about some very strange thing — maybe a non-entity — and denying something of it. Otherwise, what is the sentence about?" Reconstruct and evaluate this reasoning using the chapter's distinction between grammatical form and logical form. What has gone wrong, and what kind of philosophical mistake does the chapter say follows from such a mistake?
problems.correctAnswer:
The student is reading the sentence by its grammatical surface, as if it had the same logical structure as an ordinary subject-predicate claim like "Smith is a very capable lawyer." On that reading, "nothing" appears to function like a name for some peculiar item, and the sentence seems to attribute to that item the property of being a square circle. But this is exactly the confusion the chapter warns against. Logical form need not coincide with grammatical form. Once we notice that, the pressure to posit a strange object disappears.

The proposed consequence is incoherent for two reasons given in the text. First, if anything were a square circle, then the original statement would be false; so the sentence cannot be taken as committing us to something that is a square circle. Second, the very idea of a "non-entity" is absurd: it tries to treat what is not anything as though it were a thing. So the student's reading generates absurdity only because it mistakes grammar for logic.

According to the chapter, this is a paradigm case of bad metaphysics: people start with an obviously correct claim, think an absurd consequence follows, accept that consequence, and then invent ad hoc hypotheses about reality to preserve both. The proper cure is analysis of the statement, not ontologizing.
problems.explanation: Tests the Fregean point that grammatical form can mislead about logical form. A strong answer must show why the sentence does not commit us to a strange object and connect the mistake to the chapter's diagnosis of ad hoc metaphysical theorizing.
problems.hint: Use the chapter's sequence: correct belief, absurd consequence, acceptance of the absurdity, then ad hoc ontology.

problems.prompt: A chemistry professor tells a philosopher: "I investigate what matter is actually like. You philosophers do the same thing at a more general level — you study the most general facts of the actual world." Using the chapter's contrast between science and analytic philosophy, explain why this description is misleading. Frame your answer around a concrete example of how analyzing statements bears on possibility rather than merely cataloguing actuality.
problems.correctAnswer:
The professor's description is misleading because the chapter insists that philosophy is not a super-science adding another layer of facts about the actual world. Its task is to delineate categories and make explicit the conditions under which claims even make sense. In that respect philosophy studies possibility before actuality: by analyzing statements, it asks what could be true, since only statements that can be true make sense.

The difference is not merely one of degree. Science is chiefly interested in what is actually the case and uses possibilities instrumentally. Philosophy asks what it would even mean for something to be the case. That is why the chapter describes philosophy as metaknowledge: not knowledge of more objects, but knowledge about the forms and preconditions of knowledge.

A concrete example is "nothing is a square circle." A superficial reading might suggest some bizarre item, but analysis shows that this appearance is generated by grammar rather than logical form. The philosopher's job is not to discover whether the actual world contains non-entities, but to show that the very supposed possibility is incoherent. So philosophy clarifies the space of sense and possibility within which factual inquiry operates, rather than competing with science in describing actual reality.
problems.explanation: Tests the analytic turn from actuality to possibility and philosophy as metaknowledge. A strong answer must distinguish philosophy from science in terms of analyzing sense and possible truth-conditions, not merely studying more general facts.
problems.hint: Bring in the motorist/engineer/physicist/philosopher comparison if helpful.

problems.prompt: Dana is an anti-Platonist. She says: "Properties are nothing over and above aggregates of the things that have them. So the property of being the world's greatest harpsichord player just is the aggregate of its instances." Her friend replies with the Max case: Max is both the world's greatest harpsichord player and the only red-haired person who ever sets foot in house X. Use this case to assess Dana's view. Then explain why uninstantiated properties create an even deeper problem for her position.
problems.correctAnswer:
The Max case shows that co-extensive properties need not be identical. By stipulation, exactly one individual falls under both properties: Max. So if properties were just aggregates of their instances, the property of being the world's greatest harpsichord player and the property of being the only red-haired person to set foot in house X would collapse into the same aggregate, namely Max. But the chapter insists they are obviously different properties. One concerns musical excellence; the other concerns hair color and a relation to a house. So the aggregate theory cannot distinguish properties that share all their instances.

The problem becomes even sharper with uninstantiated properties. Suppose there are no perfectly spherical objects and no perfectly triangular objects. Then, on the aggregate view, each property corresponds to the same null aggregate. But perfect sphericality and perfect triangularity are plainly distinct. Likewise, being a perfect husband and being a perfect soldier remain different even if neither is instantiated. So anti-Platonism cannot explain either distinct co-extensive properties or distinct uninstantiated properties.

The lesson is that properties cannot be identified with spatiotemporal aggregates of their instances. We need properties themselves as non-spatiotemporal entities, with instances in space-time but not reducible to them.
problems.explanation: Tests the anti-reduction argument against identifying properties with aggregates of instances. A strong answer must use both co-extensive and uninstantiated cases to show why distinct properties would wrongly collapse.
problems.hint: Make sure to distinguish sameness of instances from sameness of property.

problems.prompt: In a logic tutorial, someone proposes paraphrasing "squareness is a form of rectangularity" as "everything square is rectangular," and concludes that property-talk is dispensable. Another student replies: "If there were only two square things, x and y, and both were green, then 'everything square is green' would be true, but 'squareness is a form of greenness' would still be false." Explain why this reply matters. What does it show about the difference between talking about properties and talking only about their instances?
problems.correctAnswer:
The reply matters because it shows that a universally quantified statement about instances is not equivalent to a higher-order statement about properties. "Everything square is rectangular" says that every instance of squareness is also an instance of rectangularity. But "squareness is a form of rectangularity" says something directly about one property standing in a relation to another property. Those are different claims.

The green example reveals the gap. If the only square things are x and y, and both happen to be green, then it is true that everything square is green. But that does not make greenness a genus or form under which squareness falls. Greenness and squareness are distinct properties, and the accidental fact that all actual square things are green cannot turn one into a form of the other. So extensional agreement among instances is too weak to capture the higher-order structure expressed by the original sentence.

This supports the chapter's broader claim that logic is property-based, not merely set-based or instance-based. Some statements are about properties themselves and cannot be paraphrased away without loss. A satisfactory analysis must preserve that higher-order content rather than replacing it with a materially equivalent claim about the current distribution of instances.
problems.explanation: Tests the distinction between first-order claims about instances and higher-order claims about properties. A strong answer must show why coextensiveness of instances does not preserve the property-level relation asserted in the original sentence.
problems.hint: Emphasize that the second sentence is about a relation between properties, not just about what objects happen to satisfy them.

problems.prompt: A classmate says: "The proposition that Tommy is smoking can just be the set {being identical with Tommy, being smoking}. If both of those properties are instantiated, the proposition is true." Using the chapter's worked analysis, show why this set is insufficient. Then explain why the chapter adds a third property and how that solves the problem without collapsing into an arbitrary truth-condition match like the bizarre set Z.
problems.correctAnswer:
The two-member set is insufficient because the instantiatedness of its members does not guarantee that Tommy is smoking. The property of being identical with Tommy can be instantiated simply because Tommy exists, and the property of smoking can be instantiated because someone else, say Larry, is smoking. So both properties may be instantiated even in a situation where Tommy is not smoking. That means the set fails to capture the proposition's truth-condition.

The chapter therefore introduces a third property: being identical with something that is smoking and is identical with Tommy. This property is instantiated exactly when Tommy is smoking. Call the individuative property A, smoking B, and the synthesizing property C. Then if C is instantiated, A and B are instantiated; and the original proposition is true iff C is instantiated. So the proposition can be modeled by the set {A, B, C}, whose members are jointly instantiated exactly when Tommy is smoking.

This is not arbitrary, unlike the set Z that includes irrelevant necessarily instantiated properties. Z may have the same truth-condition, but its members do not align naturally with what we know about the proposition's constituency. S does: one member individuates Tommy, one is smoking, and one combines them. That is why S, not just any truth-conditionally equivalent set, is the right candidate.
problems.explanation: Tests the argument that propositions are sets of properties with a genuine combinatory member, not just any truth-conditionally equivalent set. A strong answer must explain both the insufficiency of {A,B} and the constituency-based reason for preferring S over Z.
problems.hint: Ask yourself: could Tommy exist and smoking be instantiated without Tommy's smoking?

title: Unit 1 Test — The Analysis of Analysis
instructions: Timed test. Answer each question thoroughly and in your own words.

problems.prompt: A student says: “The sentence ‘Nothing is a square circle’ must be about some peculiar object—maybe a non-entity—that has the property of being both square and circular. Otherwise the sentence wouldn’t have a subject.” Reconstruct what has gone wrong using the lecture’s distinction between grammatical form and logical form, and explain why the student’s interpretation leads to absurdity.
problems.correctAnswer: The student is mistaking grammatical form for logical form. Grammatically, “Nothing is a square circle” looks like an ordinary subject-predicate sentence, as if “nothing” named some item and the rest attributed a property to it. But the lecture’s point is that this surface appearance is misleading. If we follow it slavishly, we are pushed into the absurd view that the sentence concerns some special thing—a “non-entity” or featureless un-thing—that is a square circle or perhaps at least a circle. That is incoherent in two ways identified in the text. First, if anything were a square circle, then the original sentence would be false, since it says that nothing is. Second, the very idea of a non-entity functioning as a subject is absurd: there is no such thing for a predicate to attach to. So the problem is not with reality but with bad analysis. The sentence should not be read as naming an object at all. Its real logical form expresses the impossibility of anything satisfying the combined conditions of being square and being circular in that way. The case illustrates Frege’s legacy: apparent absurd metaphysical consequences often come from failure to analyze the statement properly, not from the world containing bizarre entities.
problems.explanation: Tests the Fregean distinction between grammatical and logical form. A strong answer must show how surface grammar misleads and why reifying “nothing” or a ‘non-entity’ produces the exact absurdities noted in the lecture.
problems.hint: Ask whether the sentence requires there to be some thing for “nothing” to name.

problems.prompt: In seminar, Mira argues: “Philosophy should discover the most general facts about the actual world, just as biology discovers facts about living things. Possible cases are at best a side issue.” Using the lecture material, evaluate Mira’s claim and explain how the analytic turn changes what philosophers primarily investigate.
problems.correctAnswer: Mira’s claim reflects the pre-Fregean picture that the lecture rejects. On that older view, philosophy studies the most general features of the actual world, more or less as a highly general science. But the analytic turn changes the philosopher’s task. Philosophy does not add another body of facts to those supplied by the sciences; rather, it delineates the structures of the categories through which we already think and know. It is therefore metaknowledge: knowledge about the conditions under which claims, beliefs, and forms of understanding are possible at all. For that reason, the philosopher’s main concern is not what actually is the case, but what could intelligibly be the case. The actual matters only subordinately, because meaningful statements are those that can be true, and thus describe possible realities. Analysis of statements is therefore the route to philosophy’s subject matter. This is why the philosopher stands to the physicist as the physicist stands to the engineer: the philosopher seeks the laws governing the laws, not more first-order facts. Mira’s model treats philosophy as a rival science of extreme generality, but the lecture insists that this is mistaken. Philosophy investigates possibility, sense, and the preconditions of knowledge, not the inventory of actual reality as such.
problems.explanation: Tests the contrast between pre-Fregean philosophy and the analytic turn. A strong answer must explain philosophy as metaknowledge and why possibility, accessed through analysis of statements, is primary.
problems.hint: Use the comparison among motorist, engineer, physicist, and philosopher.

problems.prompt: An anti-Platonist says: “We don’t need properties. To say Sally and Fred are both intelligent just means they belong to the class of intelligent things. And if no perfectly triangular objects exist, then there simply is no such property as perfect triangularity.” Apply the lecture’s arguments to show why this response fails.
problems.correctAnswer: The response fails for two separate reasons stressed in the lecture. First, the ordinary predication “Sally and Fred are both intelligent” already commits us to there being something they have in common. The lecture formulates this as: there exists some property P such that Sally is an instance of P and Fred is an instance of P. This is not an optional metaphysical add-on but what the original claim requires. Replacing the property with a class of instances does not remove the need for a common factor; it merely redescribes it. Second, the appeal to classes collapses in the case of uninstantiated properties. Perfect triangularity may be uninstantiated, but it does not follow that there is no such property. If one says that because nothing has that property it does not exist, one is effectively invoking that very property in order to deny it. More importantly, anti-Platonism cannot distinguish distinct uninstantiated properties. Perfect triangularity and perfect sphericality would both correspond to the same null aggregate of instances, yet they are plainly different properties. The same issue appears with co-extensive properties, as in the Max example. So properties cannot be identical with aggregates or classes of their instances. The lecture’s conclusion is Platonist: properties exist and are not themselves in space-time, though their instances may be.
problems.explanation: Tests the arguments from common predication, uninstantiated properties, and collapse of distinct properties under instance-aggregation. A strong answer must use those lecture-specific objections rather than outside metaphysics.
problems.hint: Be sure to discuss both uninstantiated and co-extensive cases, not just one.

problems.prompt: Suppose a world contains exactly two square things, x and y, and both are green. A classmate concludes: “Since everything square is green, squareness must be a form of greenness.” Use the lecture’s discussion to diagnose the mistake.
problems.correctAnswer: The classmate is conflating a truth about all instances of a property with a truth about relations between properties themselves. In the described world, it is true that everything square is green, because the only square things are x and y and both are green. But the lecture explicitly warns that this does not license the claim that squareness is a form of greenness. “Squareness is a form of rectangularity” and “everything square is a rectangle” may coincide in extension across instances, yet they are not equivalent in meaning. The difference becomes clear in exactly this sort of case: from the fact that all square things happen also to be green, it does not follow that the property squareness stands to greenness as a determinable-specific relation or form-of relation. The first statement concerns a higher-order fact about one property’s place relative to another property. The second concerns only how certain spatiotemporal objects are distributed. So an instance-based or set-based paraphrase loses the distinction the original property statement expresses. The lecture’s broader point is that logic is property-based, not merely set-based: facts about which objects fall under which predicates do not exhaust facts about the properties themselves. Thus the classmate’s inference is invalid even though the universal generalization is true in that world.
problems.explanation: Tests the lecture’s claim that property discourse cannot be reduced to universal quantification over instances. A strong answer must explain why coextensiveness or accidental universal truth does not establish a higher-order relation among properties.
problems.hint: Contrast “everything square is green” with “squareness is a form of rectangularity.”

problems.prompt: A student proposes that the proposition expressed by “Tommy is smoking” could be identified with the set Z containing: (i) the property of being identical with a smoking Tommy, (ii) the property of being an even number, and (iii) the property of being three-sided if a triangle. Since Z’s members are instantiated exactly when Tommy is smoking, the student says Z is the proposition. Evaluate this proposal using the lecture’s account of propositions as sets of properties.
problems.correctAnswer: The proposal gets the truth-condition right but still fails, because the lecture’s account requires more than mere extensional fit. It is true that Z’s members are instantiated exactly when Tommy is smoking, since the latter two members are necessarily instantiated and the first depends on Tommy’s smoking. But the chapter explicitly says that infinitely many sets could match a proposition’s truth-condition in that cheap way, and that this is not enough for identity. What matters is whether the members align naturally with what we know about the proposition’s constituency. For “Tommy is smoking,” the lecture identifies three constituents: something individuative of Tommy, the property of smoking, and something that synthesizes or combines the first two. The set S satisfies this: A is the property of being identical with Tommy, B is smoking, and C is the property of being identical with something that is smoking and identical with Tommy. C combines A and B because it is instantiated exactly when they are jointly instantiated. Z does not display that structure. Its extra members are irrelevant to the proposition’s content and do not correspond to constituents of the proposition. So even though Z has the same truth-condition, it is not the proposition that Tommy is smoking. The account distinguishes genuine propositional structure from accidental extensional equivalence.
problems.explanation: Tests the chapter’s distinction between matching a proposition’s truth-condition and matching its constituency. A strong answer must explain why S works and Z does not, using the ideas of combination and natural alignment with constituents.

title: Homework 2 — Philosophy of Language
instructions: Untimed practice. Answer each question in a few complete sentences, in your own words.

problems.prompt: A student claims in seminar: “Literal meaning just is what speakers mean by their utterances. After all, if everyone uses ‘snow is white’ to mean that snow is white, then that sentence’s meaning consists in those speaker-intentions.” Another student replies by introducing the sentence “the cube root of three is Sir Lawrence Olivier’s favorite irrational number between one and four,” noting that it has a determinate meaning even if no one has ever uttered it. Evaluate the first student’s claim using the chapter’s arguments, and explain whether the second student’s reply is sufficient on its own.
problems.correctAnswer:
The first student’s claim confuses linguistic meaning with psychological meaning. The chapter distinguishes these sharply: psychological meaning concerns what a speaker intends to convey, whereas linguistic meaning is the literal content assigned to an expression by the language. The never-uttered cube-root sentence is a direct problem for the student’s thesis, because it appears to have a determinate literal meaning despite the likely fact that no speaker has ever used it to mean anything. So literal meaning cannot consist in what speakers have meant in uttering the sentence.

But the stronger argument is even better. When we say that “snow is white” means that snow is white, and that the cube-root sentence means what it does, the word “means” is being used in the same linguistic sense. So the relation between sentence and meaning must be the same in both cases. Since the relation cannot be speaker’s meaning in the never-uttered case, it cannot be speaker’s meaning in the ordinary case either.

Also, speaker’s meaning presupposes linguistic meaning. If I sincerely utter “snow is white” to communicate that snow is white, I can do so only because I take the sentence already to mean that. Thus the second student’s example is powerful, but by itself it is best completed by the uniformity argument and the parasitism claim.
problems.explanation: Tests the distinction among evidential, psychological, and linguistic meaning, especially the argument that literal meaning cannot be reduced to speaker’s meaning. A strong answer must use both the never-uttered-sentence point and the stronger same-relation/parasitism considerations.
problems.hint: Ask whether a sentence could have literal meaning even if no one ever intended anything by uttering it.

problems.prompt: Maria is trying to sketch the layout of a machine she has been studying. She says, “I can see exactly how the parts fit together, and I know the difference between this arrangement and that one, but I can’t yet put it into words.” Her classmate replies: “Then you don’t really know it. If you can’t say it, you don’t know it.” Using the chapter’s discussion, assess the classmate’s objection.
problems.correctAnswer:
The classmate’s objection should be rejected. The chapter argues that we sometimes grasp thoughts we cannot readily articulate and sometimes must think hard in order to find words for what we already think. That order is important: if articulation requires prior searching and reflection, then the thought cannot simply consist in a sentence of a natural language. Maria’s case fits that pattern exactly. She has a cognitive grasp of the machine’s arrangement before she can formulate it verbally.

The chapter also emphasizes that knowledge can be manifested non-linguistically. A person may show knowledge of differences and relations by drawings, movements, or other performances. Maria’s sketching is therefore not a second-rate substitute for knowledge; it is one possible manifestation of genuine understanding. The classmate’s suggestion that this is only “pseudo-knowledge” is treated as obviously false.

There is also a deeper reason. If all genuine knowledge had to be already linguistic, then we could not account for language learning or language use, since both require prior discriminatory knowledge of sounds, marks, and perceptible patterns. So Maria’s inability, for the moment, to verbalize her thought does not show absence of thought. It supports the chapter’s conclusion that language enhances cognition but does not constitute thought.
problems.explanation: Tests the argument against the thesis that thinking consists in natural-language sentences. A strong answer must use the ‘beyond articulation’ argument and the point that non-linguistic manifestations can express real knowledge.
problems.hint: Focus on the order: does finding words come after the thinking, or constitute it?

problems.prompt: Suppose Bob in fact uniquely invented Velcro and is intelligent. A student argues: “Since Bob is the inventor of Velcro, ‘Bob is intelligent’ and ‘The inventor of Velcro is intelligent’ say the same thing. The description just picks out Bob.” Evaluate this argument using the chapter’s account of definite descriptions, and explain what the second sentence really says.
problems.correctAnswer:
The student’s argument fails because it assumes that a definite description functions like a proper name. The chapter denies this. Although “Bob is intelligent” and “The inventor of Velcro is intelligent” have similar grammatical form, their logical forms differ. A proper name refers to an individual, so “Bob is intelligent” is true iff Bob has intelligence. But a definite description is not a referring term at all.

According to the chapter’s rule for definite descriptions, “the phi has psi” says that something uniquely has phi, and any such thing has psi. So “The inventor of Velcro is intelligent” means: there exists exactly one inventor of Velcro, and whoever uniquely invented Velcro is intelligent. This is false if nobody invented Velcro, false if more than one person did, and true only if there is a unique inventor and that person is intelligent.

That shows the two sentences differ in truth-conditions. Even if Bob is in fact the unique inventor, we can describe a situation in which Bob is intelligent but someone else invented Velcro; then “Bob is intelligent” is true while “The inventor of Velcro is intelligent” is false. Since difference in truth-conditions is difference in meaning, the description cannot simply be another name for Bob. Its meaning is given contextually, through the whole sentence.
problems.explanation: Tests Russell’s theory of descriptions: definite descriptions are not referring terms, and their logical form differs from grammatical form. A strong answer must state the contextual truth-conditions and contrast them with those of a proper name.
problems.hint: Ask what happens if no one, or more than one person, invented Velcro.

problems.prompt:
Compare these two arguments:

A. “No mammal is intelligent if it has pointy ears. Smith is a pointy-eared mammal. Therefore Smith isn’t intelligent.”

B. “Jones is intelligent if he has pointy ears. Smith is a pointy-eared mammal. Therefore Smith isn’t intelligent.”

They look superficially similar because each first premise has the form ‘... is intelligent if ... has pointy ears.’ Explain why A is valid and B is not, using the chapter’s lesson about grammatical form, logical form, and formalization.
problems.correctAnswer:
The two arguments are surface twins but logical opposites. The chapter’s central lesson is that grammatical form may diverge from logical form, and valid reasoning often depends on uncovering the latter. In argument A, the first premise is not about some individual becoming intelligent under a condition. It says, in effect, that for any x, if x is a mammal and x has pointy ears, then x is not intelligent. Once formalized that way, the second premise says Smith is one such x, so the conclusion follows. The inference can therefore be shown to instantiate a universally valid quantified pattern.

Argument B is different. Its first premise concerns Jones alone: if Jones has pointy ears, then Jones is intelligent. That tells us nothing directly about Smith. The second premise is about Smith’s being a pointy-eared mammal, but there is no bridge from Jones to Smith. So the conclusion that Smith is not intelligent does not follow.

The point is precisely Frege’s: syntax at the surface can conceal radically different logical forms. Formalizing an inference means exhibiting its associated conditional as an instance of an open-sentence all of whose instances are true. A can be formalized in that way; B cannot. So A is valid, whereas B merely resembles it grammatically.
problems.explanation: Tests Frege’s idea that logical form can diverge from grammatical form, especially in quantified reasoning. A strong answer must show that A is really universal and about any pointy-eared mammal, while B is singular and only about Jones.
problems.hint: Try paraphrasing A with ‘for any x’ before comparing it to B.

problems.prompt: In the 1600s, Earth-Smith and Twin-Smith are atom-for-atom duplicates and produce exactly the same noise-token: “When people are thirsty, they find it more refreshing to drink cool, glacial water than warm, swamp water; and if there were no clean water, people couldn’t survive.” Neither knows any chemistry, and both have indistinguishable thoughts and behavior. A student says: “Then their utterances must mean the same, because meaning is fixed entirely by what is in the speaker’s head.” Using the chapter’s Twin-Earth discussion, assess this claim.
problems.correctAnswer:
The student’s claim is exactly what semantic externalism denies. The chapter’s point is not that thought is irrelevant to meaning, but that meaning has an important non-psychological dimension. Earth-Smith and Twin-Smith are stipulated to be psychologically and behaviorally indistinguishable, and they produce the same noises. Even so, their utterances need not mean the same thing, because the reference of key terms can depend on the external environment.

Here the crucial term is “water.” On Earth, the substance in lakes, glasses, and bathtubs is H2O, and that is what “water” refers to. On Twin-Earth, the corresponding liquid is XYZ, not H2O. So although Smith and Twin-Smith are internally alike and may be trying to convey parallel things, the specific utterance-token on Earth concerns water, that is, H2O, whereas the corresponding Twin-Earth utterance concerns the Twin-Earth liquid, XYZ.

This shows that sameness of inner state is insufficient for sameness of linguistic meaning. A competent speaker can be ignorant of the chemistry and still successfully refer. Newton did not need to know that water is H2O for his use of “water” to refer to water. Thus what a word means is not determined wholly by what the speaker can introspect. Environmental facts partly fix semantics.
problems.explanation: Tests Putnam’s Twin-Earth argument for semantic externalism. A strong answer must explain why internally identical speakers can nonetheless utter expressions with different meanings because reference is environmentally fixed.
problems.hint: Distinguish ‘same psychology’ from ‘same reference.’

title: Unit 2 Test — Philosophy of Language
instructions: Timed test. Answer each question thoroughly and in your own words.

problems.prompt: Dana says, "Literal meaning just is what speakers intend to communicate. If no one has ever used a sentence, it cannot already have a meaning." Her classmate replies by inventing the sentence, "the cube root of three is Sir Lawrence Olivier’s favorite irrational number between one and four," and says it still seems perfectly meaningful even if no one has ever uttered it. Evaluate Dana’s claim using the lecture’s arguments. In your answer, explain whether the case merely shows an exception, or whether it undermines the identification of linguistic meaning with speaker’s meaning more generally.
problems.correctAnswer:
Dana’s claim should be rejected. The invented sentence has a determinate linguistic meaning even if no speaker has ever uttered it, so its having that meaning cannot consist in what speakers have meant by uttering it. That already refutes the thesis that literal meaning is identical with speaker’s meaning. But the lecture gives a stronger point: the word “means” in “snow is white means that snow is white” and in the cube-root sentence is being used in the same sense. So the relation between a sentence and its linguistic meaning must be one and the same in both cases. Since in the never-uttered case that relation cannot be constituted by speaker intention, it cannot be constituted by speaker intention in the ordinary case either.

The mistake is to treat coincidence as constitution. Sometimes what a speaker means and what the sentence literally means line up. But that does not show that literal meaning is made out of speaker meaning. In fact, speaker meaning presupposes linguistic meaning. If I sincerely use “snow is white” to say that snow is white, I must already take the sentence to mean that snow is white. So psychological meaning depends on linguistic meaning, not vice versa.
problems.explanation: This tests the distinction between linguistic and psychological meaning and the argument from never-uttered sentences. A strong answer must use both the simple counterexample and the stronger "same relation" argument, plus the claim that speaker meaning is parasitic on literal meaning.
problems.hint: Ask what relation the never-uttered sentence bears to its meaning, and whether that can be a relation involving actual acts of meaning by speakers.

problems.prompt: A violin teacher tells a student: "You don’t really know the difference between these two bowing techniques unless you can state the difference in words." The student cannot describe the difference verbally, but reliably demonstrates it by producing the right motion and correcting others’ mistakes. Using the lecture material, assess whether the teacher’s conclusion follows. Be sure to connect your answer to the chapter’s argument against the view that all thought is in a natural language.
problems.correctAnswer:
The teacher’s conclusion does not follow. The lecture explicitly rejects the idea that if you cannot say something, you do not know it. The student’s reliable performance and correction of others show a genuine grasp of a difference, even if it is not yet verbally articulable. That is exactly the kind of case used against the thesis that thought consists in tokens of a learned public language such as English.

The argument is that we sometimes grasp thoughts we cannot readily put into words, and we sometimes have to think in order to find words. That order matters: if one must first think and then search for an expression, the thought cannot simply be the words themselves. The student’s practical discrimination between the two bowing techniques is therefore evidence of non-linguistic cognition, not "pseudo-knowledge."

The teacher’s position is also unstable for the reason given in the lecture: language-learning itself depends on non-linguistic discriminatory capacities. One must already be able to distinguish sounds, marks, movements, or other perceptible features in order to connect words with them. So if the student’s demonstrable discriminatory ability did not count as knowledge, linguistic knowledge would lose its own foundation. Language may enhance the student’s ability to reflect and communicate, but it does not constitute the underlying thought.
problems.explanation: This tests the first argument against natural-language thought: we can think beyond articulation. A strong answer must apply the anti-articulation argument and explain why non-linguistic discrimination is bona fide knowledge, not pseudo-knowledge.
problems.hint: Use the lecture’s sequence: grasp thought first, then search for words.

problems.prompt: A museum guide says, "The founder of this museum is generous," and a visitor replies, "So you’re just saying of one particular person that he is generous, the way 'Bob is generous' says of Bob that he is generous." Suppose in fact that no one uniquely founded the museum because three people jointly did so. Using Russell’s treatment from the lecture, explain what the guide’s sentence really says and whether the visitor’s assimilation to a proper name is correct.
problems.correctAnswer:
The visitor’s assimilation is incorrect. On Russell’s analysis, a definite description like "the founder of this museum" is not semantically on a par with a proper name like "Bob." The sentence "The founder of this museum is generous" does not simply attribute generosity to some particular individual designated by the description. Its logical form is instead quantificational: it says that there exists exactly one founder of the museum, and any such founder is generous.

That is why the sentence comes out false in the case described. If no one uniquely founded the museum because three people jointly did, then the uniqueness condition fails. The sentence is therefore false, even if all three founders are generous. By contrast, "Bob is generous" would be true just in case Bob is generous; it does not build in an existence-and-uniqueness requirement concerning some property.

This difference shows that definite descriptions are not referring terms in the way proper names are. Their meaning is given contextually, by specifying the truth-conditions of whole sentences containing them. So the guide’s sentence is not about one specially named individual; rather, it says that the property of being a unique founder is instantiated and that any such individual is generous. The visitor mistakes grammatical appearance for logical form.
problems.explanation: This tests Russell’s Theory of Descriptions and the divergence of grammatical from logical form. A strong answer must reconstruct the sentence using existence and uniqueness conditions and show why the proper-name model fails.
problems.hint: Consider what happens to the sentence if there is no unique founder.

problems.prompt:
Compare these two arguments:

1. "No mammal is intelligent if it has pointy ears. Smith is a pointy-eared mammal. Therefore Smith isn’t intelligent."
2. "Jones is intelligent if he has pointy ears. Smith is a pointy-eared mammal. Therefore Smith isn’t intelligent."

A student says both have the same logical form because each starts with a sentence of the shape "___ is intelligent if ___ has pointy ears." Using the lecture’s conception of formalization, explain why this student is wrong and why the first argument can be made valid while the second cannot.
problems.correctAnswer:
The student is wrong because surface grammar does not settle logical form. Frege’s central lesson is precisely that grammatical form may diverge from logical form, and formalization requires finding a re-expression whose grammar matches the underlying logic. In the first argument, the sentence "No mammal is intelligent if it has pointy ears" is not about one individual at all. It is a quantified generalization: roughly, for any x, if x is a mammal and x has pointy ears, then x is not intelligent. Together with "Smith is a pointy-eared mammal," the conclusion about Smith follows.

That means the corresponding conditional of the inference can be shown equivalent to an instance of a true open-sentence form involving quantification. So the inference is formalizable as valid.

The second argument lacks that structure. "Jones is intelligent if he has pointy ears" concerns Jones alone: if Jones has pointy ears, then Jones is intelligent. From that and the fact that Smith is a pointy-eared mammal, nothing follows about Smith’s intelligence. The argument therefore cannot be turned into an instance of a universally true form.

So the lesson is not merely that one argument is valid and the other invalid, but why: the first premise of argument 1 must be reparsed as quantified, whereas the first premise of argument 2 remains singular. Formalization exposes this hidden difference.
problems.explanation: This tests Frege’s idea that logical form can diverge from grammatical form and that formalization shows validity by finding a true open-sentence form. A strong answer must contrast the quantified reanalysis of argument 1 with the singular structure of argument 2.
problems.hint: Ask whether the first premise is about Jones-like individuals or about all mammals with pointy ears.

problems.prompt: In 1650, Earth-Smith and Twin-Smith are atom-for-atom duplicates. They have matching thoughts, feelings, behavior, and utter the same noise: "If there were no clean water, people couldn’t survive." On Earth the liquid in lakes and glasses is H2O; on Twin-Earth it is XYZ. A critic says: "Because the two speakers are psychologically identical and mean the same thing by their words, the utterances must have the same meaning." Using the lecture’s Twin-Earth discussion, evaluate the critic’s claim.
problems.correctAnswer:
The critic’s claim should be rejected. The point of the Twin-Earth case is that sameness of psychology, behavior, and even uttered noise does not guarantee sameness of linguistic meaning. Smith’s utterance token and Twin-Smith’s utterance token differ in meaning because the word "water" in each environment refers to a different substance. On Earth, "water" refers to the substance actually found in the relevant paradigm cases—bathtubs, lakes, drinking glasses—and that substance is H2O. On Twin-Earth, the corresponding environmental substance is XYZ. So although the two men are internally indistinguishable, the semantics of their utterances diverges.

This shows the non-psychological dimension of meaning. What one thinks helps determine meaning, but it does not determine it by itself. A competent speaker can be ignorant of the chemistry of water; Newton could have used the word correctly without knowing that water is H2O. Reference is not fixed by what the speaker can internally specify.

Thus the two utterances are not the same in meaning merely because the speakers are subjectively alike. That is exactly the thesis of semantic externalism: some determinants of what our expressions mean lie outside us, in our relation to the environment and the substance our linguistic community has been tracking.
problems.explanation: This tests semantic externalism via Putnam’s Twin-Earth case. A strong answer must explain why psychological identity is insufficient for sameness of meaning and why environmental reference makes the utterances diverge semantically.
problems.hint: Focus on the word "water": what fixes its reference according to the lecture?

title: Homework 3 — Knowledge & Epistemology
instructions: Untimed practice. Answer each question in a few complete sentences, in your own words.

problems.prompt: A student says: “I knew the last digit of Professor Kuczynski’s phone number was 3. I got it right on the multiple-choice question.” When pressed, she explains that she had never seen the number before and just picked (b) at random. Another student also answered 3, but only because he had read the number on a course handout the day before. Analyze both cases using the chapter’s account of knowledge. Who, if anyone, knew the answer, and why?
problems.correctAnswer:
On the chapter’s initial analysis, knowledge requires at least true belief plus justification. Both students have a true belief, since 3 is in fact the correct last digit, and both believe it. The difference is justification. The first student arrived at the true answer by a lucky guess. Her belief is true only accidentally, so it does not count as knowledge. The chapter’s phone-number example is designed precisely to show that a correct multiple-choice answer is not enough: if one gets the truth by chance, one lacks knowledge.

The second student is different. He has a reason for believing that the last digit is 3: he read the number on a handout. That gives him justification. Assuming the handout was accurate and he remembers it correctly, his belief is not merely true but justified, and so it qualifies as knowledge on the chapter’s analysis.

This contrast also shows why not all true beliefs are knowledge. Truth alone is insufficient. What matters is whether the truth was reached through an appropriate source of justification rather than by accident. In the first case, the route to truth is epistemically defective; in the second, it is not.
problems.explanation: This tests the justified-true-belief analysis and the distinction between accidental truth and justified belief. A strong answer must explain why lucky guessing falls short even when it produces a true belief.
problems.hint: Ask whether the student had any good reason for the answer apart from luck.

problems.prompt: Nina says, “I know Bob has cancer because all red-haired people have cancer, and Bob has red hair.” In fact, Bob really does have cancer, but Nina’s general claim about red-haired people is false. Using the chapter’s discussion, assess whether Nina knows that Bob has cancer. Explain what goes wrong or does not go wrong in her reasoning.
problems.correctAnswer:
Nina does not know that Bob has cancer, even though her conclusion happens to be true. The chapter explicitly treats this kind of case: a person may reason from a false premise to a true conclusion, but when that happens the truth is reached accidentally. Nina’s belief that Bob has cancer is therefore not properly justified.

At first glance, her reasoning may seem structured and even deductively valid in form: if all red-haired people have cancer, and Bob is red-haired, then Bob has cancer. But justification depends not only on inferential form; it also depends on the credibility of the premises. Nina’s key premise is spurious. Since it is false, it cannot provide genuine justification for the conclusion. Her true belief is contaminated by misinformation.

The important point is that knowledge is not simply true belief produced by any chain of reasoning whatsoever. A true conclusion derived from a false or epistemically bad basis does not count as knowledge, because the believer has arrived at the truth in the wrong way. Nina has stumbled onto a truth, but she does not know it. Her case illustrates why philosophers add justification to truth and belief, and why not every apparent justification is real justification.
problems.explanation: This tests the chapter’s claim that spurious reasons and false premises can yield true beliefs without yielding knowledge. A strong answer must show that accidental truth through false premises is not knowledge.
problems.hint: Consider the difference between a valid argument and a genuinely justifying one.

problems.prompt: During a late-night discussion, Leo says: “Maybe everything around me is a dream. Maybe there is no keyboard, no room, no external world at all. But if that is possible, then maybe I do not even exist.” Reconstruct how a Cartesian foundationalist would respond to Leo. Which doubt is supposed to work, which is supposed to fail, and why?
problems.correctAnswer:
A Cartesian foundationalist would grant part of Leo’s skepticism but deny the rest. Descartes allows that doubt about the external world is possible. Leo may be dreaming or hallucinating, so his belief that there is a keyboard, a room, and an external world is not indubitable. That is precisely why skepticism about sense-perception becomes a serious philosophical problem.

But Descartes argues that Leo cannot coherently doubt his own mind’s existence. The reason is that doubting is itself a mental act. If Leo doubts, wonders, or thinks, then there must be a thinker engaging in those activities. So the attempt to doubt the existence of one’s own mind defeats itself. Doubt about the external world is not self-undermining in that way; from the mere fact that I seem to see a keyboard, it does not follow that a keyboard exists. By contrast, from the fact that I doubt, it does follow that there is a doubting mind.

So the Cartesian response distinguishes two targets. External objects can be doubted because appearances may mislead. The existence of one’s own mind cannot be doubted, because the very act of doubting presupposes it. That is why Descartes treats self-knowledge as privileged and foundational.
problems.explanation: This tests the cogito and the contrast between doubting the external world and doubting one’s own mind. A strong answer must explain the self-undermining character of doubting mind.
problems.hint: Ask what must already be true in order for doubting to occur at all.

problems.prompt: Mara argues: “For thirty-five years I have drunk tap water without getting sick, so the glass in front of me will not make me sick. That is obviously good reasoning, because nature is uniform: the future tends to resemble the past.” Use the chapter’s presentation of Hume to evaluate Mara’s defense. Why does appealing to the uniformity of nature create a problem?
problems.correctAnswer:
Hume would agree that Mara’s inference is not deductive. Even if she has never gotten sick from tap water in the past, it is still possible that this particular glass will make her sick. So the conclusion does not follow with necessity from the premise. That means the inference, if reasonable at all, must be inductive.

Mara then tries to justify the induction by invoking the uniformity principle: nature is regular, the future resembles the past, and so past experience is a guide to what will happen next. According to Hume, however, this move does not solve the problem. The uniformity principle is not directly known simply by perceiving this one glass or one’s own past experiences. If it is known at all, it must itself be supported by inference from previous regularities.

But that means the defense of induction already presupposes induction. Mara is saying, in effect, that past uniformities show that nature is uniform, and therefore justify projecting from past to future. That is circular. The very kind of reasoning under dispute is being used to vindicate itself. So on Hume’s analysis, appealing to nature’s uniformity does not justify induction; it merely restates inductive practice in a more general form.
problems.explanation: This tests Hume’s circularity objection to justifying induction by the uniformity principle. A strong answer must show why UP would itself need inferential support and so cannot non-circularly ground induction.
problems.hint: Ask whether the claim that nature is uniform is known directly, deductively, or only by the same kind of reasoning under question.

problems.prompt: An empiricist in class says: “All knowledge comes from sense-perception. We only ever need particular things we can see and touch. Universals like greed, humanity, or theft are just optional abstractions; explanation could do without them.” Use the chapter’s argument to assess this claim by discussing a concrete explanation such as: “Max stole the money because he is greedy and amoral and believed it was to his advantage.”
problems.correctAnswer:
The chapter’s argument is that the empiricist claim fails because explanation itself presupposes universals. In the example about Max, the explanation does not merely point to a particular object here and now. It classifies Max under characteristics such as greed and amorality, and it relates his action to kinds such as money, theft, and strategic advantage. Those are universals or properties, not merely bare particulars. Without them, the statement would cease to explain anything.

Perception, however, gives us only particulars: this person, this action, this event at this time. It does not sense-perceive greed itself or theft itself as universals. And the chapter argues that universals are not spatiotemporal entities and so cannot be causally perceived the way ordinary objects are. Since evidence through perception depends on causal interaction, there can be no observational basis for universals in the empiricist sense.

That creates the problem. If empiricism were right, we would have no good reason to posit universals. But thought, language, and explanation are saturated with them. The Max example shows this vividly: to explain why he stole the money, we must appeal to properties under which he falls. So the right conclusion, according to the chapter, is not to eliminate universals but to reject strict empiricism.
problems.explanation: This tests the argument from the particularity of perception to the indispensability of universals in explanation. A strong answer must connect the concrete explanatory case to the broader anti-empiricist conclusion.

title: Unit 3 Test — Knowledge & Epistemology
instructions: Timed test. Answer each question thoroughly and in your own words.

problems.prompt: A student says: "I knew the last digit of Professor Kuczynski’s phone number was 3. I picked 3 on the multiple-choice question, and it turned out to be right." When asked why she chose 3, she says: "No reason really—I just had a hunch." Another student also chose 3, but says he had seen the number on a departmental handout the day before. Analyze both cases using the chapter’s account of knowledge. Does either student know the answer? Explain by applying the chapter’s conditions and its treatment of justification.
problems.correctAnswer:
On the chapter’s initial analysis, knowledge requires at least truth, belief, and justification. In both cases the students believe that the final digit is 3, and in the scenario that belief is true. So the issue is justification. The first student does not know the answer, because her true belief is true only by luck. The chapter’s phone-number example is designed precisely to show that a lucky correct answer on a multiple-choice test is not knowledge. A mere hunch, with no supporting reason, is not a source of justification.

The second student is different. He believes the answer, the belief is true, and he has a reason: he saw the number on a departmental handout. That fits the chapter’s idea of justification as arising from a legitimate source, presumably perceptual evidence from reading the handout and memory of having done so. Unless there is some defeating complication, his belief counts as justified.

So the first student has a true belief without knowledge, while the second plausibly has knowledge. The contrast shows why not every true belief is knowledge: truth reached accidentally does not suffice, whereas truth reached through an appropriate justificatory route can qualify as knowledge.
problems.explanation: This tests the justified-true-belief framework and the distinction between lucky true belief and knowledge. A strong answer must identify truth and belief in both cases, then show why only the second has a genuine source of justification.
problems.hint: Ask whether the truth was reached by accident or by a reason the chapter recognizes as justificatory.

problems.prompt: In a seminar, Maya says: "For all I know, I am dreaming that I am sitting at this desk. So I can doubt that there is really a desk here. But that same possibility also shows that I can doubt that I exist, because maybe the whole thing is unreal." Reconstruct and evaluate her reasoning from the perspective of Descartes as presented in the chapter. Which part of her claim survives Cartesian doubt, and which part fails?
problems.correctAnswer:
Descartes would agree with the first half of Maya’s claim but reject the second. He allows that beliefs about external objects are dubitable. If Maya might be dreaming or hallucinating, then her belief that there is a real desk before her is not indubitable. This is exactly the skeptical pressure Descartes takes seriously in Meditation 1: sense-perception may fail to establish that the external world is as it appears.

But Descartes’ crucial point is that this doubt does not extend to the existence of Maya’s own mind. The very act of doubting is itself a form of thinking, and thinking requires a thinker. So if Maya says, "Perhaps I do not exist," the performance of entertaining that doubt already guarantees that there is a mind having the doubt. Doubting the external world is not self-undermining; doubting one’s own existence as a thinking being is.

So the surviving result of Cartesian doubt is privileged self-knowledge: Maya may not know that a desk exists, but she cannot coherently doubt that she exists as a thinking subject while she is doubting. Her mistake is to assume that the dream possibility undermines inner awareness in the same way that it undermines beliefs about external things.
problems.explanation: This tests the cogito and the contrast between dubitable external-world beliefs and indubitable self-knowledge. A strong answer must show why doubt about mind is self-undermining while doubt about the external world is not.
problems.hint: Focus on what must be true in order for the doubting itself to occur.

problems.prompt: Owen argues: "Induction is rational because nature is uniform. After all, it has always worked before: the sun has always risen, metal has expanded when heated, and water has quenched thirst. So we can trust future cases to resemble past ones." Using Hume’s argument as presented in the chapter, explain why this defense of induction is problematic. Identify the role of the uniformity principle and where the circularity appears.
problems.correctAnswer:
Hume’s challenge is that Owen’s defense relies on exactly what it is supposed to justify. The conclusion Owen wants is that inductive inference is rational: from past regularities we may infer future regularities. To support this, he appeals to the uniformity principle, the claim that nature is sufficiently uniform so that the future resembles the past and the unknown resembles the known.

The problem is that this principle is not directly known. Owen directly knows, at most, that certain regularities have held in cases already observed: previous sunrises, previous heated metals, previous experiences of water relieving thirst. But the stronger claim—that unobserved and future cases will continue to match observed ones—goes beyond what is given.

Could UP be established deductively? No. It is not a contradiction to suppose that the sun will fail to rise tomorrow or that some future sample of water will be contaminated. So the defense cannot be deductive. Could it be established inductively? Owen’s phrase "it has always worked before" does just that: it infers from past success to future reliability. But then induction is being justified by appeal to a principle whose only warrant would itself be inductive. That is the circularity Hume identifies.
problems.explanation: This tests Hume’s anti-inductive argument, especially the uniformity principle and the charge of circularity. A strong answer must explain why past success cannot non-circularly justify the move from observed to unobserved cases.
problems.hint: Separate what is directly observed from the stronger claim that future and unobserved cases will resemble the observed ones.

problems.prompt: A strict empiricist says: "All we ever need are the particular things we sense. Explanations can be given entirely in terms of concrete events, without positing universals like greed, humanity, or theft." Using the chapter’s argument, assess this claim by discussing the example: "Why did Max steal the money? Because Max is greedy and amoral and believed it was to his strategic advantage." Why does the chapter think the empiricist cannot preserve explanation while rejecting universals?
problems.correctAnswer:
The chapter’s objection is that explanation is saturated with universals. In the Max example, the explanation does not merely point to a sequence of bare particulars. It classifies Max under kinds or characteristics: greed, amorality, belief, strategic advantage, theft, and money. Those are not just this-here-now sensory particulars; they are universals or properties under which particulars fall.

The empiricist proposal fails because sense-perception gives only particulars, whereas explanation requires general features, categories, and natures. To explain why Max stole the money is to say more than that one event followed another. It is to cite characteristics and principles associated with those characteristics. Without universals, the explanation loses its intelligibility: it no longer tells us why this action made sense given Max’s traits and beliefs.

The chapter goes further: this is not an accidental feature of one example but a structural feature of explanation as such. The very idea of an explanation that dispenses entirely with universals is said to be incoherent. Thus if empiricism denies any non-perceptual access to universals, it undermines the conditions of thought, language, and explanation. That is why the chapter concludes that strict empiricism is indefensible.
problems.explanation: This tests the argument from the particularity of perception to the indispensability of universals in explanation. A strong answer must show that explanatory discourse classifies particulars under properties and cannot be reduced to mere sensed particulars.
problems.hint: Look at the nouns and adjectives doing explanatory work in the Max example.

problems.prompt: Lena says: "I know Bob has cancer because all red-haired people have cancer, and Bob has red hair." In fact, Bob really does have cancer, but the premise about red-haired people is false. Apply the chapter’s discussion of spurious reasons to determine whether Lena has knowledge. Then explain what this case shows about why justified true belief requires more than merely arriving at a true conclusion.
problems.correctAnswer:
Lena does not know that Bob has cancer, even though her conclusion is true. The chapter explicitly treats this sort of case: a person reasons from a false generalization—"all people with red hair have cancer"—to the true conclusion that a red-haired friend has cancer. The belief ends up true, but the route to it is spurious.

This matters because the chapter’s motivation for adding justification to true belief is not satisfied by any old reason. A reason can appear to support a conclusion while actually being false or defective. When that happens, the truth of the conclusion is accidental relative to the believer’s grounds. Lena’s belief matches reality, but not because her evidence or reasoning connects her appropriately to that reality. She has stumbled onto the truth through misinformation.

So the case shows that knowledge excludes accidentally true belief. It is not enough that one believes a truth and can cite some argument for it; the support must be genuine rather than spurious. False premises can generate true conclusions, but when they do, the resulting true belief does not amount to knowledge. The example sharpens the point that epistemic success must not be a matter of luck masquerading as justification.
problems.explanation: This tests the chapter’s treatment of spurious justification: true belief based on false premises is not knowledge. A strong answer must explain that the truth is accidental relative to the believer’s grounds, not properly connected to them.
problems.hint: Ask whether the belief is true because of the reason offered, or merely true despite it.

title: Midterm Examination — Units 1–3
instructions: Timed midterm covering Units 1–3. Answer each question thoroughly in your own words.

problems.prompt: A biology student says: "Science tells us what kinds of animals exist. Philosophy should discover a special set of philosophical facts over and above biology, psychology, and physics. Otherwise philosophy contributes nothing." Another student replies: "That gets philosophy wrong. When we ask what a person, a fact, or knowledge is, we are not adding new items to the inventory of the world; we are making explicit the conditions something must satisfy to fall under categories we already use competently." Using the lecture’s account of philosophy, analyze which student is closer to the truth and explain what role the distinction between knowledge and meta-knowledge plays here.
problems.correctAnswer:
The second student is closer to the lecture’s view. On that view, philosophy is not one more science contributing a further stock of first-order facts alongside biology or physics. Its task is to delineate categories: person, statement, fact, knowledge, value-judgment, and so on. That means making explicit the structural conditions something must meet in order to count as a member of one of those categories. We already think and act through such categories, but usually without an explicit theory of them.

The key distinction is between knowledge and meta-knowledge. We often know how to apply a category while being unable to say what it is. For example, we can judge many cases of linguistic behavior or moral conduct correctly while struggling to state the principles embodied in those judgments. Philosophy addresses that gap. It gives knowledge about the categories through which ordinary and scientific knowledge operate.

So philosophy does contribute something, but not by adding a new region of facts. It clarifies the preconditions and logical structures of the concepts already presupposed by every inquiry. In that sense it is “the analysis of analysis” or “the science of science”: reflective understanding of the framework within which other disciplines already proceed.
problems.explanation: Tests the chapter’s conception of philosophy as metaknowledge rather than a producer of extra first-order facts. A strong answer must explain category-delineation and the gap between competent use and explicit articulation.
problems.hint: Ask whether philosophy studies the same objects as the sciences, or the conditions for applying the categories used in any inquiry.

problems.prompt: Dana argues that the proposition expressed by "Tommy is smoking" can be identified simply with the set containing two properties: being identical with Tommy, and smoking. Eli objects that this leaves something out. Reconstruct the lecture’s argument for Eli’s objection by describing a case in which Dana’s proposal fails, and explain why a third property is needed.
problems.correctAnswer:
Eli is right according to the lecture. If the proposition "Tommy is smoking" were just the set containing (A) being identical with Tommy and (B) smoking, then its truth would amount merely to A and B both being instantiated. But that is too weak. There is an obvious countercase: Tommy exists and is not smoking, while Larry is smoking. In that situation A is instantiated, because Tommy exists; and B is instantiated, because someone is smoking. Yet the proposition "Tommy is smoking" is false.

So the set {A, B} does not capture the proposition’s truth-condition. We need a further property that supplies the right synthesis between Tommy and smoking. The lecture introduces (C): being identical with something that is smoking and is identical with Tommy. This is the property whose instantiation guarantees not merely that Tommy exists and that smoking occurs somewhere, but that the smoker is Tommy.

Hence the proposition must at least include A, B, and C. More generally, the point is that atomic propositions require not only an individuative component and a predicative component, but also a property encoding their connection. Without that synthesis, the account cannot distinguish the true proposition from worlds where the relevant properties are instantiated separately.
problems.explanation: Tests the chapter’s argument that propositions are sets of properties and that atomic propositions need a synthesizing property, not just subject and predicate properties. A strong answer must present the Larry/Tommy-style failure case.
problems.hint: Imagine a world where Tommy exists and smoking occurs, but not by Tommy.

problems.prompt: In a seminar, Mira says, "Bill’s hacking cough means he has a lung infection, because the infection caused the cough." Theo replies, "Causation can matter, but that cannot be the whole story. A failed exam can be caused by drunkenness without being evidence of drunkenness, and slurred speech can be evidence of poor performance without causing it." Apply the lecture’s distinction about evidential meaning to evaluate both speakers.
problems.correctAnswer:
Theo’s response matches the lecture more closely. In the evidential sense of “means,” x means y when x is evidence of y. Causation is related, but the relation is neither necessary nor sufficient.

It is not necessary because evidence can run in patterns other than direct causation. A cause can be evidence of its effect: Bill’s current drunkenness can be evidence that he will perform poorly on the exam. Also, two effects of a common cause can be evidentially related: Bill’s slurred speech can be evidence of poor exam performance even though the slurring neither causes nor is caused by the poor performance; both stem from the drunkenness.

It is not sufficient because even if y caused x, x counts as evidence of y only when one cannot reasonably suppose that some other cause produced x. Bill’s failing a test may in fact have been caused by drunkenness, but that failure is not thereby good evidence of drunkenness, since there are many plausible alternative causes of failure.

So Mira is partly right that causal facts often underwrite evidential meaning, but wrong to identify the two. Evidential meaning is a broader epistemic relation governed by what reasonably supports what, not a simple causal relation.
problems.explanation: Tests the distinction between evidential meaning and causation. A strong answer must show both directions: causation is not necessary and not sufficient for evidential meaning.
problems.hint: Use both of the lecture’s Bill examples, not just one.

problems.prompt: A student claims that if Bob in fact invented Velcro, then "Bob is intelligent" and "The inventor of Velcro is intelligent" say the same thing, since they concern the same person. Using the lecture’s analysis of definite descriptions, show why this is mistaken by giving a concrete scenario and reconstructing the logical form of the description sentence.
problems.correctAnswer:
The claim is mistaken because co-reference does not guarantee sameness of meaning. On the lecture’s analysis, a definite description of the form “the phi” does not function like a proper name. “The inventor of Velcro is intelligent” means: something uniquely invented Velcro, and any such thing is intelligent. That sentence therefore builds uniqueness and existence into its content.

A concrete scenario shows the difference. Suppose Bob is intelligent, but in fact no one invented Velcro, or alternatively two people jointly invented it, or a single unintelligent person other than Bob invented it. In those scenarios, “Bob is intelligent” may still be true, but “The inventor of Velcro is intelligent” is false. It is false if there is no unique inventor, and false if the unique inventor is unintelligent.

So even in a world where Bob actually is the unique inventor, the two sentences have different truth-conditions. The proper name sentence attributes intelligence directly to Bob. The definite-description sentence says that there exists exactly one inventor of Velcro and that whoever uniquely satisfies that description is intelligent. Since the truth-conditions differ, the meanings differ. This is precisely why grammatical similarity should not mislead us about logical form.
problems.explanation: Tests Russell-style analysis of definite descriptions and the divergence between grammatical and logical form. A strong answer must give the quantified content and explain the truth-condition difference from a proper name sentence.
problems.hint: Ask what happens if nobody or more than one person invented Velcro.

problems.prompt: Earth Oscar and Twin Oscar are molecule-for-molecule alike, behave the same way, and inwardly feel exactly the same. On each planet, each points to the clear liquid in lakes and says, "Water fills this pond." A classmate argues: "Since their psychology is identical, their word 'water' must mean the same thing." Another replies: "The lecture says meaning has an external dimension, so sameness of psychology is not enough." Evaluate the dispute using the Twin-Earth argument as presented.
problems.correctAnswer:
The second classmate is right on the lecture’s view. The point of Twin-Earth is precisely that the semantics of a term can differ even when the speakers are psychologically and behaviorally indistinguishable. Earth Oscar and Twin Oscar may have the same internal states, the same dispositions, and the same subjective experiences when using the word “water,” yet their utterances can mean different things because meaning is partly fixed by factors external to the speaker.

The argument does not deny that psychology matters. It says rather that psychology does not settle meaning by itself. The lecture emphasizes a non-psychological dimension to linguistic meaning. So if the clear liquid on Earth and the corresponding liquid on Twin-Earth differ, then what Earth Oscar refers to with “water” can differ from what Twin Oscar refers to, even though neither could tell the difference from the inside.

That is semantic externalism. The determinant of what their word means is not exhausted by what is in their heads. Therefore the inference from “same psychology” to “same meaning” is invalid. The Twin-Earth case is designed to show exactly this possibility: perfect internal duplication without semantic identity.
problems.explanation: Tests semantic externalism through the Twin-Earth case. A strong answer must state that identical psychology/behavior does not guarantee sameness of meaning because semantic determinants can be external.
problems.hint: Do not say thought is irrelevant; the lecture says only that it is not sufficient by itself.

problems.prompt: An empiricist in class says: "All knowledge comes from sense-perception. If you cannot see or otherwise perceive something, you cannot know it. So talk of non-spatiotemporal properties is empty." A Platonist classmate accepts the lecture’s ontology of properties and replies that strict empiricism cannot accommodate that ontology. Using only the lecture material, explain why the Platonist is committed to rationalism and what pressure strict empiricism faces.
problems.correctAnswer:
The Platonist classmate is right by the lecture’s reasoning. Strict empiricism says all knowledge derives from sense-perception. But the lecture also holds that properties are not in space-time, even though spatiotemporal things instantiate them. We perceive property-instances in things, but not the properties themselves as spatiotemporal objects. So if one accepts a Platonic ontology of non-spatiotemporal properties, one cannot consistently maintain that all knowledge comes through the senses alone.

That is why Platonism commits one to rationalism. Rationalism need not deny the importance of perception; it claims only that some knowledge has a non-perceptual basis. Knowledge of properties, especially uninstantiated or non-spatiotemporal ones, requires such a basis. Otherwise one would have to deny that we know anything about them, or deny that they exist.

The lecture further argues that strict empiricism is unstable. If pursued consistently, it collapses either into skepticism or Berkeleyan idealism. The pressure arises because our commerce with the world presupposes resources not simply given in sensation. Thus the empiricist’s challenge to non-spatiotemporal properties rebounds against empiricism itself: either it abandons the ontology, or it must concede that sense-perception does not exhaust the sources of knowledge.
problems.explanation: Tests the link between Platonism and rationalism, and the lecture’s critique of strict empiricism. A strong answer must explain why non-spatiotemporal properties cannot be known by perception alone.
problems.hint: Connect the metaphysical claim about properties to the epistemological claim about the sources of knowledge.

title: Homework 4 — Metaphysics, Mind & Modality
instructions: Untimed practice. Answer each question in a few complete sentences, in your own words.

problems.prompt: A student says: “Yesterday the weather app predicted sunshine at 2 p.m., but at 2 p.m. it rained. So the atmosphere must be indeterministic. If the future had really been fixed, the app could have gotten it right.” Using the chapter’s distinction between determinism and predictability, evaluate this argument. In your answer, explain why a deterministic system can still resist full prediction, and connect that point to the lecture’s discussion of perception.
problems.correctAnswer:
The student’s argument confuses determinism with predictability. Determinism is the claim that the state of the world at a time fixes the entire later course of events. Predictability is a different matter: whether some knower can correctly forecast those later events in advance. The chapter explicitly says that the converse from unpredictability to indeterminism fails. A system may be deterministic and yet not fully predictable.

So the failed weather prediction does not show that the atmosphere was undetermined. It shows only that the predictor lacked perfect access to the relevant state, or that prediction from that state was not available to the predictor. The stronger point in the lecture is that this is not merely a practical defect of current technology. Perception itself introduces a logical gulf. Our information about external things comes through processes such as light, and those processes take time and alter what they interact with. Thus any perceptual state represents how things were a little earlier, not exactly how they are now. If prediction depends on current information, and current information is always already dated, then complete prediction is impossible even in a deterministic world.

Therefore the app’s failure is no evidence for indeterminism. Apparent irregularity is not the same as metaphysical openness.
